title: Turn a Grid Clockwise
statement:
You get a square grid grid of integers with n rows and n columns. Turn it a quarter turn clockwise, the way an image viewer rotates a photo to the right.

Change grid in place and return nothing. Do not build a second n × n grid; aim for O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: The left column, read bottom to top, becomes the top row: 3, 1. Turning the other way would give [[2, 4], [1, 3]].
Only transposing (flipping across the diagonal) gives [[5, 8, 7], …]: each row comes out backwards. Transpose, then reverse every row.
A single cell is its own rotation.

gen: (r, big) => { const n = big ? 20 : r.int(1, 6); return [r.matrix(n, n, -9, 9)]; }
hints: Track one cell. Where does the value at row i, column j end up after a clockwise quarter turn?
It lands at row j, column n − 1 − i. That is two simpler moves combined: swap row and column, then mirror left to right.
Transpose in place by swapping grid[i][j] with grid[j][i] for j > i only, then reverse each row.

explain.intuition:
Follow one cell. After a clockwise turn, the value at (i, j) sits at (j, n − 1 − i). That formula is two easy moves glued together. Transposing sends (i, j) to (j, i). Reversing each row then sends column i to column n − 1 − i. Both are simple swaps inside the grid, so no second grid is needed.

It is the same trick CSS uses when rotate(90deg) is built from a reflection and a flip: two mirrors make a rotation. Turning counter-clockwise uses the same two moves with the other reversal (reverse each column, or reverse rows first).
steps: For every pair with i < j, swap grid[i][j] and grid[j][i]. This transposes the grid.
Reverse each row in place with two pointers from its ends.
Nothing to return: the grid itself now holds the turned image.
pitfalls: Swapping across the diagonal for every (i, j), not just j > i. Each pair gets swapped twice and the grid ends up unchanged.
Reversing the order of the rows instead of each row's contents. That gives a counter-clockwise turn.
Writing grid = rotated inside the function. That only rebinds the local name; the caller's grid never changes.

solutions.title: Build a turned copy, then copy it back
solutions.idea: Write each value straight to its new spot (j, n − 1 − i) in a fresh grid, then copy that grid over the original. Simple, but it uses O(n²) extra memory.

solutions.title: Transpose, then reverse every row
solutions.idea: Mirror across the main diagonal, then mirror each row left to right. Two reflections make a quarter turn.

solutions.title: Rotate four cells at a time, ring by ring
solutions.idea: Each cell in the outer ring trades places with three partners, one on each side. Move all four in one cycle, then move inward.

followups: Turn it counter-clockwise instead. Which of the two steps changes?
The grid is m × n, not square. Why can't you do it in place any more, and what would you return?
Turn it by 180°. Is there a single-step way?
